articles.title_zh: China’s First Distributed In-Hold Dredge Pump Equipped Ultra-Large Self-Propelled Dredger “Xin Hai Jing 1” Delivered
articles.content_orig:
It's on us. Share your news here.
Posted on October 27, 2026
On October 23, the “Xin Hai Jing 1,” China’s first extra-large self-propelled trailing suction hopper dredger designed with distributed in-hold dredge pumps, built by Shanghai Zhenhua Port Machinery (ZPMC) for CCCC Shanghai Dredging, was officially delivered at ZPMC Qidong Offshore Engineering base. The vessel achieves full-chain independent controllability of dredging equipment—from overall design to core components—and combines intelligent operation with green, low-carbon advantages. It will support major marine engineering projects and inject strong marine engineering momentum into the building of a maritime power.
It is reported that this vessel was constructed under a turnkey contract by the National Engineering Research Centre of Dredging and designed by the Marine Design and Research Institute of China (MARIC). With a maximum hopper capacity of 27,929 m³ and a maximum dredging depth of 120 meters, the vessel’s performance, environmental standards, and technical capabilities all rank among the world’s best, marking China’s achievement of full autonomy and control over the entire dredging equipment supply chain—from overall design to core components.
The “Xin Hai Jing 1” has an overall length of 180 meters, a beam of 36 meters, and a draft of 17.2 meters. Breaking away from the traditional centralized layout of mud pumps on cutter-suction dredgers, it is the first vessel to install two in-hold mud pumps in separate forward and aft pump compartments at the front and rear of the mud hold, respectively. This innovative hydrodynamic layout addresses the challenges of pipeline resistance and center of gravity balance in ultra-large vessels under extreme operating conditions, significantly enhancing stability and dredging efficiency under various loading conditions, and filling a gap in the design and application of distributed in-hold dredge pumps in China’s dredging industry.
Full-chain domestic production is the most outstanding achievement of the “Xin Hai Jing 1.” Centering on the requirements for ultra-large dredging depth, ultra-strong soil-breaking capability, and ultra-long discharge distance, all parties involved ine thconstruction adhered to demand-driven development and mobilized more than 110 domestic suppliers for collaborative research and development. Together they developed a series of core dredging-specific equipment, including a high-capacity, high-efficiency universal draghead suitable for both deep and shallow water, a lightweight 120-meter deep-water long drag arm system, and a high-efficiency hopper loading and overflow device. These efforts have driven a large number of core dredging-specific equipment items to complete domestic verification and supporting application, establishing a complete closed loop covering design and R&D, system integration, core supporting equipment, and full-scale ship verification, effectively shoring up shortcomings in China’s dredging and reclamation industry chain.
Intelligence and green development are the distinctive hallmarks of the “Xin Hai Jing 1.” The vessel is equipped with a new-generation intelligent monitoring and integrated management platform fully independently developed by China, adopting a “1 platform + N systems” architecture that enables fully automated control of “one-key dredging,” “one-key spoil dumping,” and “one-key reclamation,” and achieves “dredging-navigation integration” and even “unmanned dredging” under typical operating conditions.
Its digital twin system and “digital sentinels” based on AI vision and LiDAR can intelligently identify safety hazards such as smoke, flames, and oil leaks, with a recognition accuracy of over 95%. Both the main and auxiliary diesel engines are equipped with SCR denitrification systems. Through comprehensive measures including distributed in-hold dredge pumps, optimized pipeline layout, streamlined hull form for drag reduction, hybrid drive, and intelligent power and energy efficiency management, the vessel achieves a carbon emission reduction of more than 20% and a dredging efficiency improvement of approximately 30% compared with conventional vessels of the same type.
Once delivered and put into service, the vessel will be widely deployed for major projects such as deep-sea sand dredging, deep-water port and channel dredging along the coast, land reclamation, and coastal protection. It will further strengthen the capabilities of China’s ultra-large cutter suction dredger fleet and continue to advance the localization and iterative development of key supporting components, as well as the research and development of a series of related equipment.

articles.title_orig: Stock futures are little changed after Wall Street starts the week on a winning note: Live updates
articles.title_zh: Stock futures are little changed after Wall Street starts the week on a winning note: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
The tech industry needs this to go well. So does Wall Street.
Anthropic's IPO filing on Monday puts the Claude creator in position to pursue what could be the largest initial stock offering in history. Investors are already measuring the 5-year-old company's potential market cap in the trillions, putting it in a category with the world's most valuable companies.
It's a critical moment for the whole tech sector, as the artificial intelligence boom has been largely driven by two companies: Anthropic and OpenAI. The latter has confidentially filed to go public, but has said a debut likely won't take place until 2027.
Meanwhile, the stock market is showing signs of jitters on the AI trade. Neoclouds and data center companies have been getting pummeled, prompting Australia's Firmus to withdraw its IPO plans and for SK Hynix's U.S.-based Solidigm unit to do the same.
Now, all eyes turn to Anthropic , which is betting that investors will look past over $80 billion in losses in the first half of the year, and see the 14-fold increase in revenue as a reflection of seemingly insatiable demand for the company's leading models and services.
"If it underperforms expectations, it'll be a little bit of a house of cards," said Jai Das, co-founder of Sapphire Ventures whose career in tech investing dates to the 1990s.
Anthropic's business is deeply entwined with tech megacaps. Close to half its revenue comes from Claude being sold through cloud divisions at Microsoft , Amazon and Alphabet , which all hold investments in the company. In the IPO, some $77 billion in notes can be issued to Amazon , Broadcom and Google , while Microsoft and Nvidia agreed to invest $15 billion as the company builds up its computing capacity. Chips from Nvidia, Advanced Micro Devices , Amazon and Google are powering Anthropic's development.
Cloud providers are ratcheting up capital expenditures to meet demand, and memory manufacturers are fighting shortages to prioritize AI chips. And there's the debt factor. Alphabet, with its investment-grade credit rating, committed to backstopping Anthropic for a data center in Texas. Broadcom , which helps Google develop chips for AI labs, is creating financing pools to help Anthropic and OpenAI deploy high-performance models, CEO Hock Tan told analysts earlier this year.
For public market investors, more than one-third of the value of the S&P 500 comes from tech's trillion-dollar companies, which are all, to varying degrees, going deep in AI. Beyond that, there are software giants like Adobe and Salesforce that have integrated with Anthropic's Claude assistant.
And in the private markets, check sizes have ballooned but IPOs are few and far between. Bessemer Venture Partners and Menlo Ventures both told CNBC that Anthropic is their biggest investment ever.
"If they don't perform well, they will become the bellwether for AI," said Brad Bernstein, a managing partner at growth equity firm FTV Capital. "Their valuation will reflect that performance variation, and then it'll just be a trickle-down effect to all the stuff going on with the excess capital that's getting poured into the venture AI world. Everything is going to have to sort of be reset."
Anthropic will be the third company to go public with a valuation above $1 trillion, after Saudi Aramco and Elon Musk's SpaceX , which debuted in June. OpenAI could be the fourth.
Revenue at Anthropic has been multiplying at a staggering pace as businesses adopt the company's coding and productivity tools. Second-quarter revenue soared to $11.56 billion from $787 million a year earlier.
The company held almost $132 billion in cash, equivalents and short-term investments at the end of June. And after five quarters of operating losses, Anthropic reported $974 million in operating income for the second quarter.
"It is, I think, better than feared," said Rohit Kulkarni, partner and chief AI officer at Burnham Park Capital Markets, referring to the financials. "There could have been more negative tidbits."
One source of concern in some corners of the investing universe is the emergence of so-called open-weight models, which are cheaper for businesses to access and allow for customization and flexibility in terms of where users access the models.
In the prospectus, the only two competitors Anthropic named were OpenAI and Google, though the company said it faces competition from a "broader set of model providers," including open-weight or open-source models.
Anthropic says it's all very early, with Fortune 500 companies committing less than 0.1% of their total expenses to its models and services in the latest quarter. Michael Monaghan, portfolio manager at Founder ETFs, says that's part of the investment thesis.
"I think there's going to be room for frontier models like Anthropic and OpenAI and SpaceX, and I think there will be room for open-weight models," Monaghan said. "It's way too soon to say that one is going to disintermediate the other."
With hyperscaler spending on AI infrastructure set to reach into the trillions of dollars, Sapphire's Das said there's understandable concern about a market glut. But he compares it to the telecommunications and dot-com bubble of the late 1990s, when companies flooded the market with fiber-optic equipment. Eventually, the infrastructure got used, although plenty of companies went belly up in the interim.
"Long term, I don't think there is a lack of demand," Das said.
A lackluster debut could push out OpenAI's offering even further and cause investors to rethink its lofty valuation. At the same time, rising interest rates mean it's getting costlier for companies to raise debt.
David Trainer, CEO of financial research firm New Constructs, wrote in a report last month that the AI boom has been built on the view that cheap credit and access to the capital markets will be "readily available."
"If AI liquidity dries up, and there are clear signs it is, we see large, 20%, downside risk in the S&P 500, with most of that concentrated in the valuation of AI-related stocks," Trainer wrote.
Industry experts take a different approach, focusing on the power and rapid proliferation of the technology. Claude Opus 5.5 Max performs better than any other model on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, an industry benchmark .
Snowflake CEO Sridhar Ramaswamy said the technology is only becoming more essential.
"Anthropic and OpenAI have by now demonstrated their ability to stay at the frontier of AI and keep pushing innovation," Ramaswamy said. "They're incredible companies that are doing a big service to humanity by expanding the frontier of what is possible, and we are very much rooting for them to be public and very successful companies."
Still, Snowflake is experimenting with low-cost open-weight models from China's Moonshot AI, DeepSeek and Zhipu.
"We spend a lot on internal AI because we want to get as much efficiency as we can," Ramaswamy said.

articles.title_orig: FTC and 20 states sue Dollar General, accusing bargain chain of overcharging customers
articles.title_zh: FTC and 20 states sue Dollar General, accusing bargain chain of overcharging customers
articles.content_orig:
Suit that cites 2025 Guardian investigation alleges ‘pattern of inaccurate pricing’ that ‘affects millions of purchases’
The Federal Trade Commission and 20 states have sued Dollar General, the nation’s largest dollar-store chain, for persistently overcharging customers at its more than 20,000 stores across the United States.
The lawsuit , filed in federal court in Nashville, cites a Guardian investigation published last December.
“Dollar General has for years engaged in deceptive conduct that harms the very consumers it claims to serve,” the 95-page legal complaint claims.
“Although Dollar General promises convenience, low prices, and value, the company has routinely charged customers more at the register than the prices displayed on shelves, price tags and advertisements. This pattern of inaccurate pricing has persisted for years and affects millions of purchases across the country.”
The lawsuit says the scope of the retail chain’s “pricing misconduct” is “staggering”.
The FTC is the federal agency charged with protecting consumers from deceptive, unfair and anticompetitive business practices. State authorities from Mississippi to Ohio to Nebraska to Utah have joined the case as plaintiffs.
Dollar General pushed back against the allegations.
“The lawsuit filed today ... suggests that we have abandoned our mission and willfully disregarded the affordability needs of our customers,” the company said in statement . “Nothing could be further from the truth. Our goal is 100% accuracy between shelf and register prices in every store.”
The FTC’s allegations are consistent with the Guardian’s December 2025 investigation , which found that Dollar General stores failed more than 4,300 government price-accuracy inspections in 23 states over a three-year period. That article “was the subject of significant internal deliberation and discussions” within the company, the lawsuit said.
The agency noted in the lawsuit that Dollar General has policies in place that are supposed to align register prices with shelf prices. For example, it directs employees to remove and replace outdated labels on certain days of the week. Workers told the Guardian that, because of understaffing, they are often too busy to change those labels.
“Dollar General’s on-paper policies to update pricing achieve little in practice,” the lawsuit said, because “they do not track whether the printed labels are actually affixed to shelves.”
The FTC cited a Guardian interview with a former lead sales associate in Louisiana who said: “I threw away tags sometimes, to keep me or a co-worker out of trouble.”
The lawsuit indicates that FTC investigators made undercover purchases at Dollar General stores in Ohio, Pennsylvania, Missouri and Maryland over a two and half month span. The first of these secret shopper tests took place this January, six weeks after the Guardian’s investigation focused wide attention on the discount chain’s pricing practices.
Every single undercover visit, the suit says, turned up overcharges on multiple products. At a Dollar General in Cleveland, 8 of 58 items purchased rang up more costly than the prices listed on the product label or shelf – an overcharge rate of nearly 14%.
Dollar General said it first learned of the FTC’s investigation in February when it received a civil investigative demand from the agency. The company said that the investigation appeared to have “an unusually accelerated timeline” but that it “engaged cooperatively with the commission, producing more than 200,000 documents and over 350 gigabytes of data and making several company representatives available to provide sworn testimony on relatively short notice”.
The company’s statement said it pushed back against the calculations behind the FTC’s demand for financial compensation for consumers, but that it was surprised when the agency did not respond to its counteroffer and instead filed suit.
Dollar General said it “will defend this litigation vigorously”.
The company said that, in the retail marketplace, “occasional price discrepancies can occur. When that happens, our store teams are instructed, empowered and expected to make things right for the customer. In recent years, we have enhanced our price-accuracy processes and remain committed to continuous improvement.”
In a separate case, the New York attorney general, Letitia James, announced earlier this month that Dollar General had agreed to a $1.875m deal to settle allegations that it had repeatedly overcharged customers across the state.

articles.title_orig: BlackRock’s Rieder Spent All Weekend Doing Deals in AI Debt Rush
articles.title_zh: BlackRock’s Rieder Spent All Weekend Doing Deals in AI Debt Rush
articles.content_orig:
Investors may be wary of the volatility hitting parts of the bond market right now, but they have an "historic" opportunity to grab attractive yields in high-quality credit, Rick Rieder, BlackRock's chief investment officer for global fixed income, told CNBC in an exclusive interview.
Hypothetically, it's now possible for investors to build a diversified portfolio that yields more than 7% with less than three years of duration and an average credit quality of A-, he said. Duration is a measurement of a bond's price sensitivity to fluctuations in rates, and issues with shorter maturities tend to have lower duration.
"Not only is it historic in that these yields are where they are, but the only time these yields are ever here is when there's some problem, like an economic problem or default problem," Rieder said in an interview about his fourth-quarter outlook , released Wednesday.
That isn't the case now, where the economy remains strong, he said. "So you don't really have to worry about defaults of any significance."
While Rieder didn't specifically identify the credits in the aforementioned portfolio, the iShares Aaa - A Rated Corporate Bond ETF (QLTA) has a 30-day SEC yield of 5.68% and an effective duration of 6.48 years — higher than Rieder's low duration focus.
The iShares Flexible Income Active ETF (BINC) , which is managed by Rieder, has a 5.66% 30-day SEC yield and three-year effective duration, but its portfolio extends beyond investment-grade credit.
Rieder sees the best opportunity right now in investment-grade corporate bonds — which he pointed out he hasn't said "in a really long time." Investment grade bonds are rated AAA through BBB- by S&P and Fitch, while Moody's rates them Aaa through Baa3.
That includes hyperscaler bonds, which have flooded the market with issuance this year as they ramp up their AI infrastructure. Alphabet , Amazon , Meta Platforms and Oracle have issued a total of about $228.4 billion in bonds year to date, as of Oct. 20, according to LSEG.
"They're very low leverage. They have tremendous amounts of cash flow coming in," Rieder said of the hyperscalers in general. "You're now getting to buy these entities which are higher quality, paying you a very attractive yield to get it."
Rieder's iShares Flexible Income Active ETF has upped its allocation to investment-grade corporates to 14.3% of its portfolio. In July , that stood at 8.5%.
That said, investors need to be patient and sit tight since rates could still move higher from here, he advised.
"Your starting point is by far your best barometer of what your return is going to be," he noted. "So if you get seven and a quarter, maybe you get eight, maybe you get six, but ... if your holding period is a year or longer, you're going to get that yield."
Caution should also be exercised outside of investment-grade credit, which requires more selectivity and deep research, he warned. That includes AI names.
"There's parts of the data center supply that's not hyperscaler guaranteed or hyperscaler backed," he said. "That we've been more cautious around, and we'll continue to be."
The bond market, particularly high-yield credit, has been rocked as investor concern grows over the massive amount of debt some companies are taking out to fund their artificial intelligence build-out.
Junk-rated CoreWeave has become the poster child, seeing its stock drop, bond yields jump and credit-default spreads widen. Oracle , which is sitting in the lower end of investment grade and is seen as a bellwether on the broader AI market, has also taken some hits.
Rieder is also keeping an eye on the Federal Reserve , which is expected to raise its federal funds rate again in December to combat inflation. The market is currently pricing in a nearly 90% probability that the central bank will hike at that time, according to the CME Group FedWatch tool .
The money manager expects that to happen, although he does not agree with it. Higher rates are hurting parts of the economy, like housing, while not having much of an impact on other areas — such as tech companies' capital expenditures, which have become a big driver of growth, he said.
"They're not borrowing off the overnight funds rate," Rieder noted. "There's a lot of floating rate finance in housing, credit card, auto loan finance, and you're seeing those areas already under pressure."
Instead, the market is and will continue to price the AI supply coming into the market, he added.
Rieder sees a number of possible risks ahead, including rising levels of government debt across the globe. In the United States, the budget deficit has grown to $2 trillion for fiscal 2026.
"The more the central banks raise the rates, the cost of debt to these to already indebted governments is something we've got to be careful about over time," he said.
Bond supply coming from AI companies should also be watched.
"With the amount of supply that's coming — data center, hyperscaler — there's some crowding-out effect that's taking place," he said. "With government rates moving higher, that is something that we just got to keep an eye on."
In the meantime, Rieder would just continue to reap the rewards of high investment-grade yields "and smile a lot," he said.

articles.title_orig: Modders unlock hidden AI performance on NVIDIA RTX 20, 30 and 40 series GPUs, with up to 2× tensor throughput
articles.title_zh: Modders unlock hidden AI performance on NVIDIA RTX 20, 30 and 40 series GPUs, with up to 2× tensor throughput
articles.content_orig:
Modders have found ways to remove NVIDIA’s compute performance restrictions on several generations of GeForce graphics cards. What started with the RTX 3090 series has now expanded to RTX 40 models and even the older RTX 2080 Ti.
The modifications can nearly double the throughput of certain Tensor Core operations without changing the hardware or flashing a new VBIOS. However, this does not mean twice the gaming performance, and the GeForce RTX 50 Blackwell series has yet to receive a confirmed working unlock.
The research builds on earlier attempts to unlock restricted compute capabilities on NVIDIA CMP mining GPUs. Developer Zagitta adapted these techniques for GeForce RTX 30 cards through the open-source GPU-Unlock project, while work involving TOTORONG’s firmware payload extended support to the Ada architecture.
Instead of modifying graphics drivers, the tools change low-level GPU configuration registers before the NVIDIA driver loads, removing limits on the rate at which certain Tensor Core instructions can be issued. The changes are temporary and are cleared when the GPU loses power.
The reported results are substantial in specific compute tests. An RTX 3090 Ti increased BF16 matrix multiplication performance from 87.5 to 157.4 TFLOPS, while an RTX 4090 doubled its measured FP16 Tensor Core instruction throughput from 165.6 to 331.6 TFLOPS. KohakuBlueleaf has also demonstrated an RTX 2080 Ti reaching 111 TFLOPS, compared with 59.9 TFLOPS before the unlock. That particular card was already physically modified with 22GB of VRAM, which is unrelated to the software unlock. Successful tests have also been reported on RTX 3060, RTX 3070, RTX 3080 and selected RTX 40 models, although support is not yet validated across every GPU variant.
These modifications primarily affect FP16 and BF16 operations with FP32 accumulation, alongside certain TF32 and FP8 workloads on supported architectures. They can accelerate AI tasks involving matrix multiplication, including LLM prompt processing and some image-generation workloads.
However, actual gains depend on the software being used. RTX 3090 reports show LLM prompt-processing improvements of roughly 14% to 36%, while token generation remains largely unchanged because it is often limited by memory bandwidth. Gaming performance is unaffected by these specific unlocks. Most projects currently target Linux, although experimental Windows implementations are also available. They are not risk-free, and unsupported configurations may fail to boot.
Some users are already asking NVIDIA to officially remove these restrictions from older GeForce products, many of which are no longer manufactured. That would benefit owners using their existing GPUs for AI workloads, but it raises another question for gamers. Cards such as the RTX 3090 and RTX 4090 already attract AI buyers because of their 24GB memory capacity, and improving their compute performance could make them even more attractive on the second-hand market.
So perhaps asking NVIDIA to remove these restrictions is the right call, just not at the best time. It’s hard to argue against unlocking performance on GPUs that are no longer in production and, in most cases, already out of warranty. But the GPU market is hardly in good shape right now, and making older GeForce cards more attractive to AI users could make things even worse for gamers. But can it really get any worse?
Source: RTX 30 Unlock (GPU-Unlock), RTX 40 Unlock (GPU-Unlock-Ada), RTX 20 Unlock (Turing Unlock)

articles.title_orig: Americans warned to rethink travel to 13 countries amid deadly attacks
articles.title_zh: Americans warned to rethink travel to 13 countries amid deadly attacks
articles.content_orig:
The U.S. State Department has updated travel advisories for several Middle Eastern countries , warning of potential armed attacks by Iranian-backed Houthi forces and threats targeting Americans.
Five countries — Iran, Iraq, Lebanon, Syria and Yemen — are listed under the department’s highest advisory level, Level 4, which warns Americans not to travel.
Eight others, including Israel, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates, are designated Level 3, urging travelers to reconsider their plans.
While the advisory levels largely remained unchanged, all 13 advisories were updated on Friday.
The advisories cited recent attacks by Iranian-supported Houthis, including strikes on Riyadh’s airport in Saudi Arabia and “other critical infrastructure,” the department said.
The attacks have resulted in civilian deaths and widespread travel disruptions, with the State Department warning that the hostilities “have the potential to escalate rapidly beyond that immediate area.”
Americans traveling to the region also face additional risks, including health concerns in Iraq and Yemen, officials said.
Kidnapping and hostage-taking were listed as additional concerns in Iran, Iraq, Lebanon, Syria and Yemen, according to the State Department.
Civil unrest was also cited as a risk in Iran, Iraq, Israel, Lebanon, Syria and Yemen.
The State Department encourages Americans traveling to these countries to enroll in the Smart Traveler Enrollment Program (STEP) to receive security alerts and updates from U.S. embassies.
Americans are also urged to monitor local news, prepare to shelter in place if conditions worsen and have an emergency departure plan that does not rely on U.S. government assistance.
Fox News Digital reached out to the State Department for additional information.
The updates follow several other recent travel warnings issued by the State Department.
Last week, the State Department raised its travel advisory for Kenya from Level 2, “Exercise Increased Caution,” to Level 3, “Reconsider Travel,” citing health risks, crime, civil unrest, kidnapping and terrorism.
At around the same time, officials warned Americans traveling to China of the risk of wrongful detention, electronic surveillance and restrictions that could prevent them from leaving the country.

articles.title_orig: US bans vehicles from China’s BYD at Japan military base, calling them ‘unacceptable’ risk
articles.title_zh: US bans vehicles from China’s BYD at Japan military base, calling them ‘unacceptable’ risk
articles.content_orig:
US military says the restrictions on the electric vehicles at Kadena airbase also apply to delivery drivers and taxis
One of America’s biggest overseas military bases has banned vehicles made by the Chinese electric vehicle maker BYD over security concerns, the US military in Japan said on Tuesday.
The ban, which went into effect this week at Kadena airbase on the southern Japanese island of Okinawa , has fueled speculation that similar measures could be taken at other US military facilities as part of Washington’s crackdown on Chinese technology it suspects of being used to collect sensitive information.
“These vehicles present an unacceptable and unmitigable risk to our personnel and our mission,” Lieut Col Alli Stormer, a spokesperson for the US air force 18th Wing at Kadena, said in a statement.
The restrictions apply to all BYD vehicles, including privately owned cars, taxis and delivery vehicles, reports said, adding that security personnel stationed at the base’s gates had been instructed to block BYD vehicles and instruct drivers to turn around.
Kadena, the biggest US air force base east Asia, would be directly involved in responding to a crisis involving China , Russia or North Korea .
Its inventory includes the powerful Typhon missile system, which is said to be capable of firing Tomahawk missiles as far as 1,600km, putting parts of China and Russia within striking distance. Kadena also hosts fighter planes and aircraft used for mid-air refuelling, surveillance and reconnaissance, according to its website.
The move comes amid concerns of potential information leaks via vehicle-mounted technologies such as cameras, sensors and GPS devices, South Korea’s Yonhap news agency said.
American military officials have not identified a specific threat, but the ban is part of wider measures taken by the US and other western countries to restrict Chinese smart technology in vehicles, mobile phones and other devices they fear could be used to “spy” on their owners.
In June the Pentagon added BYD to a list of 188 Chinese firms it believes have ties to the country’s military, drawing a protest from Beijing. The blacklist also includes the automaker Nio, e-commerce firm Alibaba and internet company Baidu.
The US defence department banned the sale and use of smartphones from Chinese companies Huawei and ZTE at military bases worldwide in 2018, again citing security concerns.
China has imposed similar restrictions on US-made Tesla vehicles. In 2021, it barred them from some government compounds due to security concerns over ⁠cameras installed on the vehicles. Beijing removed that restriction in 2024 after Tesla won an endorsement from the country’s top auto industry association.
BYD, which has not immediately responded publicly to the Kadena ban, overtook Tesla as the world’s biggest seller of battery-electric vehicles in 2025.
It is now expanding overseas, including in the world’s fourth-biggest auto market, Japan , where in July it launched its Racco electric minicar in the hope that the small, cost-efficient vehicle would carve out a place in a market dominated by domestic brands.

articles.title_orig: From the Mediterranean to the dinner table
articles.title_zh: From the Mediterranean to the dinner table
articles.content_orig:
Bluefin tuna does not forgive delay. The fatty belly — otoro — is prized for a richness that seems to dissolve on the tongue, a quality built on gloss, deep color and a marine intensity that no cooked fish can replicate. That pleasure lasts only as long as the cold chain holds. A few hours of warmth, a break in handling, and the texture turns from silk to something far less forgiving.
Delivering bluefin at its best is therefore an industrial problem disguised as a culinary one. The fish must move from sea to ultra-low-temperature storage quickly, in volume, and without interruption.
The Ocean Star exists for that problem. It is a floating cold-chain hub that links Maltese harvesting expertise with Chinese cold-chain capacity.
It is an ultra-low-temperature processing and transportation vessel owned by Mediterranean Bluefin Industry Development (Hainan), a China-Malta joint venture specializing in bluefin tuna processing and trade.
The joint venture was established in June 2024 by Malta Fish Farming Ltd, or MFF, and China's Shandong Far-sea Development Ltd, covering trade, transportation and processing.
The vessel began a new production season in late September, operating in the Mediterranean east of Malta.
Workers weigh tuna on its decks, move product into refrigerated rooms, and dock at Valletta Port — images that trace the journey from harvest to cold storage.
MFF Chairman Salvu Ellul described the Ocean Star as the first ultra-low-temperature refrigerated transport and processing vessel and said it had become the most efficient bluefin tuna processing platform in the Mediterranean region.
He made the remarks on Oct 11 while briefing China's Ambassador to Malta, Zhang Zuo, during a visit to the Valletta waterfront in October.
Ellul told the ambassador that cooperation between the two nations in the fisheries sector had expanded year by year and that there were high expectations the partnership would serve as a bridge for economic and trade exchanges between China and Malta.
Ellul pointed to the Belt and Road Initiative as a source of trade opportunities, saying that Malta Fish Farming would ride the wind and waves to bring Malta's highest quality bluefin tuna products to the consumers' table worldwide.

articles.title_orig: Saudi-led coalition says it intercepted Houthi missiles, drones attacking kingdom
articles.title_zh: Saudi-led coalition says it intercepted Houthi missiles, drones attacking kingdom
articles.content_orig:
The Iran-backed Houthis have been attacking critical Saudi infrastructure.
Talks between the U.S. and Iran remain stalled despite the two countries signing a memorandum of understanding in June, aimed at ending the war that began with joint American-Israeli strikes on the country in February. The opening strikes killed a host of top Iranian officials and commanders, among them Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.
The two sides have continued to exchange strikes, though have not returned to the intense fighting seen in the early stages of the conflict. The U.S. says it is enforcing a naval blockade of the country's Persian Gulf and Gulf of Oman ports, while Iran claims control over the strategic Strait of Hormuz and continues to claim attacks on shipping transiting the waterway.
Meanwhile, intensified fighting between Saudi-backed Yemeni forces and Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen has seen the latter repeatedly attack Saudi military, oil infrastructure and transport facilities.
See the most recent developments below.
The official Telegram page for Mojtaba Khamenei has released details of two meetings Iran's supreme leader has reportedly held in recent days.
According to the readout, he met with the head of Iran's judiciary, Gholamhossein Mohseni-Ejei, on Saturday, during which the two reportedly discussed pursuing compensation from the U.S. and Israel over damages from the war in Iran. That follows a meeting last week with Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, Iran's parliament speaker, during which the two reportedly discussed the latest developments in the war, according to the readout.
Khamenei has not been seen in public since he succeeded his late father in March.
Tehran will host a security summit attended by senior officials from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan, Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei told reporters on Monday.
Baqaei described the meeting as "a prelude to establishing indigenous security within the region."
Rayed Krimly, Saudi Arabia's deputy minister for public diplomacy, said in a post to X that Riyadh's delegation will include Defense Minister Khalid bin Salman.
Krimly added that Pakistani army chief Field Marshall Asim Munir and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin will also attend the meeting, which will be chaired by Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council.
-ABC News' Victoria Beaule and Somayeh Malekian
Yahya Saree, the spokesperson for the armed forces of the Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen, said on Monday morning that the group launched a new ballistic missile attack on the King Khalid International Airport in the Saudi capital Riyadh.
The attack came hours after flights resumed at the airport, having been suspended following recent and deadly Houthi strikes there.
Saudi military spokesperson Col. Turki Al-Maliki said in a post to X on Monday morning that Saudi forces intercepted a Houthi ballistic missile bound for Riyadh. Maliki also said that Saudi forces launched a series of airstrikes in Houthi-controlled Yemeni territory targeting missile storage and launch sites.
Saudi Arabia's General Directorate of Civil Defense, meanwhile, posted an advisory to X warning of potential danger to Riyadh. An hour later, the directorate said the danger had passed.
The U.S. intelligence community has gathered information through various channels indicating that Iran has "substantially increased" efforts to target American officials abroad, according to a memo sent from Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton to Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
"The lethal plotting efforts by the Iranians against U.S. citizens have reached advanced stages in both the Middle East and certain other countries," Clayton wrote.
Clayton also said that senior members of Rubio's staff had been briefed on the matter and that he would make every effort to downgrade as much of the intelligence as possible so that it could be shared more widely within the State Department.
A U.S. official confirmed the authenticity of the memo, which is unclassified and dated Oct. 23.
"When it comes to our staffing at embassies, we constantly evaluate new information about the security environment," the official said. "The threat of Houthi attacks and of Iranian terror plots targeting U.S. officials are informing our decisions on staffing adjustments for embassies on restricted operating status in the region."
The existence of the memo was first reported by Axios.
-ABC News' Shannon Kingston

AI-generated “sob-story boys” have recently taken Chinese short-video platforms by storm, allegedly using emotional manipulation to cheat elderly viewers out of their savings.
Known collectively as “Xiaohai”, these digital avatars typically appear as teenage boys in school uniforms or plain white shirts, tearfully describing their poverty-stricken lives on camera.

articles.title_orig: Dollar General overcharged millions at checkout for years, FTC and 20 states allege
articles.title_zh: Dollar General overcharged millions at checkout for years, FTC and 20 states allege
articles.content_orig:
The Federal Trade Commission and 20 states on Monday sued Dollar General, accusing the budget retailer of charging customers more for products than it advertised.
The chain, which operates 21,000 stores nationwide, allegedly mislabeled prices for years, "extracting millions of dollars in unlawful overcharges," the FTC alleged.
"Dollar General has betrayed the trust of millions of American consumers and imposed significant financial harm on communities and consumers who are already struggling to make their paychecks last," Christopher Mufarrige, director of the FTC's Bureau of Consumer Protection, said in a statement .
The FTC added that American consumers depend on Dollar General's advertised low prices to make ends meet on tight budgets, while prices that don't reflect advertised deals make it impossible for them to manage household finances.
The agency filed its complaint in the U.S. District Court for the Middle District of Tennessee, Dollar General's home state.
"Our goal is 100% accuracy between shelf and register prices in every store," Dollar General said in a statement. "As with other retailers and despite our policies and procedures, occasional price discrepancies can occur. When that happens, our store teams are instructed, empowered, and expected to make things right for the customer. In recent years, we have enhanced our price-accuracy processes and remain committed to continuous improvement."
Dollar General said it was made aware of the FTC's investigation in early February.
According to the suit, thousands of Dollar General stores unlawfully overcharged shoppers.
Dollar General "has for years engaged in deceptive conduct that harms the very consumers it claims to serve," the FTC and states allege in the suit. "Although Dollar General promises convenience, low prices, and value, the company has routinely charged customers more at the register than the prices displayed on shelves, price tags, and advertisements. This pattern of inaccurate pricing has persisted for years and affects millions of purchases across the country."
The company also faced thousands of consumer complaints claiming it failed to honor advertised prices at checkout, a sign Dollar General knowingly harmed customers, according to the FTC.
The suit seeks a permanent injunction, along with monetary and other relief.
Dollar General in its statement said, "FTC staff also demanded a monetary amount that was untethered to — and orders of magnitude larger than — any realistic assessment of amounts attributable to pricing discrepancies."
The company said it "worked tirelessly and in good faith to resolve this matter without litigation," including an "alternative, and in our view, more reasonable, manner of calculating potential settlement ranges."
"Although we respect the FTC's role in protecting American consumers and the State representatives' role in protecting the citizens of their respective states, we will defend this litigation vigorously," it said.

articles.title_orig: Trump allies fall in two elections as Netanyahu faces next test
articles.title_zh: Trump allies fall in two elections as Netanyahu faces next test
articles.content_orig:
Brazil, Israel, Serbia and the US are holding elections within the space of 10 days. Will the authoritarian right cement its global gains, or can pro-democracy forces make a comeback?
Four elections on four continents within 10 days could profoundly reshape global politics, propelling the world further along its current authoritarian trajectory or marking a limited comeback for democratic norms.
In all four contests, basic democratic norms are at stake at a time when autocracy is advancing worldwide at an alarming rate. According to the Sweden-based V-Dem Institute , which uses multivariable assessment tools, the democratic freedoms enjoyed by the average global citizen are down to levels last seen in 1978 – long before the fall of the Berlin Wall and the collapse of communism in Europe.
The cluster of four pivotal elections could either halt that trend or reinforce it. In each contest, pro-democracy parties are in close races with current or aspiring autocrats. The outcomes in each case are likely to have spillover effects in their regions and beyond.
On Sunday, Brazil will hold runoff presidential elections with a candidate from the far right in the lead. If he wins, Flávio Bolsonaro is threatening to “change the constitution”, pardon his father for plotting a coup, and ease environmental restrictions, a critical issue for the Amazon rainforest.
On the same day, the semi-autocracy run by Aleksandar Vučić in Serbia for the past 12 years will face its stiffest challenge in the form of an unconventional student-led protest movement , fielding a slate of little-known academics and technocrats running on the simple slogan “Serbia or Mafia?”.
On Tuesday, it will be the turn of Benjamin Netanyahu to face his challengers at the polls. Israel’s leader for 19 of the past 30 years has overseen a prolonged period of democratic backsliding and spiralling human rights abuses . He is wanted by the international criminal court for war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza, and risk heightened legal jeopardy from an ongoing corruption trial at home if he loses. His far-right coalition is currently trailing an opposition block.
On 3 November, at the tail end of this potentially historic 10 days, Donald Trump’s imperial-style presidency is facing a rebuke from US voters in midterm elections, with at least one chamber of Congress, and possibly two, likely to fall to the Democrats. They will then however face an uphill task in seeking to rein in Trump’s excesses which have seen the US plummet down the V-Dem Institute’s Liberal Democracy Index .
By the time the US counts its votes on Tuesday, the world could look a markedly different place. Not only are the four looming contests bunched together, they are also interwoven. Trump’s Maga movement has given overt political support to Netanyahu, Vučić, and Bolsonaro. Israeli-built Pegasus spyware has been found in the phones of student and pro-democracy activists in Serbia. Bolsonaro is strongly pro-Israel and is promising to follow the US lead and move the Brazilian embassy to Jerusalem. The US has provided much of the ordnance for Netanyahu’s wars. Serbia is committed to spending $2bn on Israeli defence systems and in September, the two countries opened a joint plant making surveillance and attack factory.
Victory for the authoritarian right in one country will bolster counterparts in others, and conversely win for pro-democratic campaigners in each contest will give hope and encouragement to their allies around the world.
The four elections may be closely interlinked, but the struggle between authoritarianism and democracy takes on very different forms in each country. The odds are different in each case, as are the stakes, but they are all close races.
Democracy Index ranking 28
Brazil has enjoyed a democratic resurgence since Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva took office on the first day of 2023, defeating an attempt by his far right populist predecessor to overturn the October election result. According to V-Dem’s measures, it now has better democratic credentials than the UK, and far better than the US.
The loser in those elections four years ago, Jair Bolsonaro, an ex-soldier who served under Brazil’s 21-year military dictatorship and still admires it, was sentenced to 27 years in jail for trying to stage a coup to hold on to power. Now his son, Flávio, is seeking to follow in his footsteps, and goes into the second round of the election on Sunday with a small but significant lead over Lula.
The younger Bolsonaro has not only pledged to free his father, but also to punish members of the judiciary involved in his prosecution. If he wins, he will have a supportive rightwing majority in Congress to work with and has vowed to change the constitution and “ re-democratise the country ”. The term harks back to the transition from military rule in 1985, and for the Brazilian left, it has a chilling Orwellian ring coming from the mouth of an avowed admirer of prominent members of the junta.
Bolsonaro has campaign on hard-line law and order policies addressing the chronic issue of high crime. He argues for lowering the age of criminal responsibility to below 18, sending more teenagers to jail, and calling for judicial reforms, which his critics suggest he intends to mount an attack on the independence of the courts.
Democracy Index ranking 112
Over his 12 years as president, Aleksandar Vučić has steadily corroded the pillars of Serbia’s democracy. He and his allies have taken over almost all the country’s broadcast channels, with the result that he is the overwhelming presence on the nation’s television screens over the course of the current election campaign. The future of the last two independent news channels is now in doubt, as they were bought during the campaign by a Portuguese investor with links to the ousted Hungarian regime of Viktor Orbán.
The ruling Serbian Progressive party (SNS) has turned ministries and other state institutions into political tools to the extent that, in the words of Raša Nedeljkov, the programme director of the Center for Research, Transparency and Accountability, “the line between the state and the parties is almost deleted”.
Until now, the opposition parties seeking to curb Vučić have been weak and divided, but Serbian politics was transformed two years ago by the collapse of a concrete canopy on a crowd of people at a railway station in Novi Sad, killing 16 people. The tragedy crystallised a deep reservoir of disillusion across the country, and produced a student-led mass movement which has survived state intimidation since then, and is now fielding a full list of candidates against the SNS.
The candidates, like the students who nominated them, disagree among themselves on key political issues but they demonstrate a purist adherence to direct democracy. Decisions are taken by large plenum meetings, and no one has been allowed to emerge as an identifiable leader.
To win on Sunday, the students will have to break the mould of Serbian politics, and in particular, Vučić’s hold on his loyal base in the countryside. If they come close, there is a risk of unrest and violence. The SNS has a record of paying bands of thugs to disrupt opposition rallies, and those gangs may appear at polling sites if Vučić feels threatened. The students too have vowed to take to the streets to defend the victory they expect on Sunday.
Democracy Index ranking 48
Israeli democracy has always been partial. Palestinians in the occupied territories do not have the vote or many other rights, while Israeli settlers next door to them are treated as full citizens and provide vital backing for Benjamin Netanyahu’s far-right coalition government. That government however will be fighting for its survival in Tuesday’s parliamentary elections.

articles.title_orig: A Damning Account Alleges Jared Kushner Conducted Diplomacy for Profit
articles.title_zh: A Damning Account Alleges Jared Kushner Conducted Diplomacy for Profit
articles.content_orig:
In late spring 2020, a source I knew to be reliable called me with a story. The Dutch government had hacked into Jared Kushner ’s phone and monitored him as he accessed a Dubai-based bank account. What was odd, the source said, was that the money in the account—hundreds of millions of dollars—had come from a bank in Azerbaijan. Most importantly, Kushner appeared to have transferred significant amounts of money from the Dubai account to other individuals, including a warlord, a mercenary and a one-time hit man. The story sounded preposterous, I told my source. And yet.
Six months later, I found myself speaking with someone else about the UAE government and their use of mercenaries in conflicts around the Middle East and Africa when I asked, on a whim, whether they knew anything about Kushner and bank transfers from a UAE account. My acquaintance grew quiet. Then they replied, “Yes.”
Over the next four years, I came to learn that, sometime in late 2017, the Netherlands Defense Intelligence and Security Service (MIVD) made a startling discovery. A General Staff of the Armed Forces of the Russian Federation (GRU) operative, a dark web hacker specializing in stolen bank data, was traveling to the UK for an espionage mission. They reached out to the British government for permission to apprehend him when he arrived. The British agreed.
When the Russian national arrived in England, the Dutch informed him that he had two options: he could work for them against the GRU, or the British would arrest him. Once in UK government custody, the operative would be charged with espionage. If convicted, he would spend years in a British prison. The Russian chose to change his employer.
Later that year, the Russian operative gave the Dutch spies access to one of the GRU’s most sensitive assets. Located in Rostov, Russia, the GRU’s hacking and cyber team operated a remote server on which they stored some of their bounty. During their search through these secret files, the Dutch found something astonishing: screenshots of Jared Kushner’s iPhone.
In The Hague, the MIVD hacking team tried to reverse engineer the Russian penetration of Kushner’s iPhone. Kushner owned what was then the latest model, the iPhone X. Released in November 2017, it featured Face ID, a state-of-the-art security feature that Apple had promoted at its launch. The Dutch team had been trying to pick the phone’s door lock, so to speak, when it occurred to them that the Russians may have found an unlocked window to gain entry instead. Their hypothesis was correct. By early 2018, the MIVD had found a vulnerability in the iPhone that gave them access. The security exploit wasn’t perfect, however. Some malware allows a hacker to turn a victim’s phone into a microphone and video camera, turn the phone on or off, and pull and add files. The Dutch solution did not provide that level of access. Instead, when Kushner used the phone, they could see his screen. Almost as soon as they got inside, the intelligence service began capturing every image of Kushner’s screen as he used it, filing their own cache of surveillance on their internal computer servers.
As they monitored Kushner’s phone, they discovered he used it to log in to a UAE bank account. By the time the Dutch spies had visibility into the phone, the account had received hundreds of millions of dollars from a bank in Azerbaijan. Their initial assessment was that the bank account was affiliated with the government there.
For the MIVD hackers, the bank account became an intelligence mystery to unravel. Nearly everything they worked on had a tinge of Russian conspiracy. A little over a year into Trump’s first presidency, the MIVD, like FBI agents and federal prosecutors in Washington working on the Robert Mueller investigation, had only part of the story.
Kushner, UAE ruler Mohamed bin Zayed (MBZ) and Mohammed bin Salman (MBS) of Saudi Arabia, converged at an auspicious moment. MBS wanted to be crown prince. MBZ wanted to blow up Obama’s Iran nuclear deal, and Kushner wanted both to help him force the Palestinians into a deal that Israel would accept. Despite the perception of his wealth, Kushner was not entirely financially independent of his parents, and the family business, Kushner Companies, faced a billion-dollar loan coming due on their trophy property, the Manhattan office building at 666 Fifth Avenue.
Early in the first Trump administration, MBZ and MBS offered to pay for a slush fund dedicated to helping the new administration with foreign policy goals. The idea was to help pay for Trump’s promised wall between Mexico and the US, for example, in an effort to secure a second term in the White House. The two Arab royals initially discussed with Kushner putting more than $10 billion into the effort. Within months, though, as MBZ pushed the Trump administration to help back MBS’s effort to become his country’s crown prince—and future king—the broader foreign policy slush fund idea fizzled. Instead, MBZ and MBS initially, and then MBZ alone, put at least $2 billion into at least two bank accounts for Kushner. It is unclear how the royals organized their $2 billion in combined payments, but they effectively split the cost. For the purposes of explanation, it is best to understand where and how each bank account was controlled.
Bank account Alpha was held at First Abu Dhabi Bank, the largest in the UAE, and was overseen by MBZ’s brother, Tahnoon bin Zayed, who served as the bank’s chairman. Beginning in 2017, the Saudis and Emiratis transferred roughly $750 million into the Alpha account. Alpha would be used as a foreign policy fund. This money would be overseen and partially managed by Kushner and MBZ, who, in their effort to strike a grand bargain to end the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, believed the region’s map needed to be redrawn.
“Jared was looking for shortcuts in his diplomacy,” a source who knew of the UAE’s deal with Kushner said. This person held discussions with both senior UAE and Israeli officials about the secret financial arrangement between Kushner, the UAE, and, at least initially, Saudi Arabia. “Jared promised MBZ that he’d push their agenda with Trump if they participated in a fund. He wanted normalization with Israel so that business could take off.” A slush fund—a shared pool of money for off-the-books diplomatic objectives—was a common form of Gulf Arab government corruption, this person explained. “The Emiratis and the Saudis do this once a year. A billion or two is nothing for them, and if it gets them what they want, it’s money well spent.”
The Alpha account looked like the funding source of a UAE government program, by which MBZ paid his bureaucrats their salaries or funded government-run schools. But how and through whom the money flowed into the Alpha account revealed that it was intended to remain secret, more akin to a covert and illicit scheme, given that it was managed in part by a senior advisor to the president of the United States.
The Dutch spies who monitored the Alpha account noted that all of it was sent by a bank in Azerbaijan in American dollars. Azerbaijan plays a unique role in money laundering. Its central bank maintains high levels of US dollars in its reserves but does not adhere to the highest standards of bank transparency. As a result, Azerbaijani banks have well-established but unadvertised practices of serving as way stations for large transfers, in which a foreign currency is exchanged for an equal amount in dollars. For a roughly 6 to 7 percent fee on the transaction, some Azerbaijani banks will accept a transfer from a client who wishes to move Saudi riyals or Emirati dirhams totaling hundreds of millions of dollars. The Saudi or Emirati client sends the money to the Azerbaijani bank, which then uses a different internal bank account to transfer the equivalent US dollars to the client’s requested destination. For auditors, this shadow trade can’t be discerned.

articles.title_orig: China and Russia are redrawing Arctic trade. Can Europe fight back?
articles.title_zh: China and Russia are redrawing Arctic trade. Can Europe fight back?
articles.content_orig:
China and Russia are tightening their grip on Arctic shipping routes, turning the rapidly warming region into a new geopolitical battleground with Europe.
Moscow and Beijing last week have agreed to expand freight traffic along Arctic shipping corridors , increase services between their ports and deepen cooperation on building polar vessels.
The agreement came after the EU unveiled a new Arctic strategy aimed at countering growing Russian and Chinese influence in the region.
Although the competing moves underscore how the once-remote region is turning into a strategic prize, analysts said that Europe's ability to challenge the emerging China-Russia partnership remains limited, given Moscow's control over the main shipping corridor and Beijing's growing commercial clout.
That's because Moscow controls the Northern Sea Route, including shipping permits, transit fees and a vast fleet of nuclear icebreakers, while Beijing provides the cargo, vessels and industrial capacity needed to develop the corridor, she added.
Europe, by contrast, has limited icebreaker capacity and Arctic infrastructure, leaving it with little leverage to challenge the partnership despite its position as a major destination market.
The Northern Sea Route offers itself as an increasingly attractive alternative, as Middle East disruptions expose vulnerabilities in established shipping corridors.
Cargo traveling between Asia and Europe through the Northern Sea Route could have its journey shortened to between 18 to 22 days, down approximately 35% from the 28 to 35 day journey through Suez, according to data provided by Fertmax FZCO.
For Moscow, the route offers an opportunity to redirect energy exports toward Asia as Western sanctions constrain its access to European markets, said industry watchers whom CNBC spoke to.
On the other hand, it provides Beijing another trade artery that could reduce reliance on traditional maritime chokepoints.
David Roche, a veteran strategist at Quantum Strategy & Geonomics, said the Arctic's importance lies less in its potential to transform global shipping than in the deepening economic dependence between Russia and China.
"The significance of the arctic route is for Russian energy shipments to China, which will increase China's control over Russia in terms of Russia's dependence on China to sell its energy to compensate for losses of its gas markets in Europe," Roche highlighted.
The EU has acknowledged the growing challenge, highlighting the region's strategic value in its strategy, as mentioned by EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas last week .
Europe isn't entirely without leverage.
The EU's new strategy calls for expanding European icebreaker capacity, strengthening maritime surveillance and developing infrastructure linking Arctic trade networks to European markets.
It also proposes a maritime security hub and greater protection for undersea cables, reflecting growing concerns about Russian military activity and threats to critical infrastructure.
Yet those strengths may not be enough to overturn the structural advantages enjoyed by Moscow and Beijing, said experts.
Garcia-Herrero said Europe's leverage largely rests on its position as a major destination market and the presence of large shipping companies that have avoided the Arctic because of environmental and commercial risks.
Europe also faces a strategic dilemma: engaging with the emerging corridor could deepen its reliance on Russian-controlled infrastructure, even as it seeks to reduce Moscow's economic influence.
Fertmax FZCO's former global head of research, Daeijin Lee said Western operators face sanctions, insurance and compliance complications that make the route considerably less attractive than it is for Chinese companies.
"The Arctic gives diversification, not independence," he said.
For all the geopolitical attention, the Arctic remains a marginal player in global shipping.
Roche estimates Arctic trade accounts for roughly 0.3% of global shipping today and could reach about 1% by 2030.
Data from Russian state nuclear corporation Rosatom and CNBC calculations based on UN Trade and Development figures similarly supports the 0.3% figure, with 37.02 million tonnes of cargo transiting the Northern Sea Route in 2025 compared to the 12.72 billion tonnes of global seaborne trade in 2024.
Only 3.2 million tonnes of that cargo, or less than a tenth, involved vessels transiting the entire route, rather than shipments originating or terminating in the Russian Arctic, according to the Centre for High North Logistics .
But traffic may be picking up, the latest September 2026 CHNL data showed.
The route recorded 104 confirmed transit voyages carrying an estimated 3.7 million tonnes of cargo by the end of September, exceeding the 3.2 million tonnes recorded during the entire 2025 navigation season.
Much of the existing traffic consists of Russian oil, liquefied natural gas and other commodities rather than international container shipments.
However, the route also faces significant commercial hurdles. Ice conditions restrict navigation for much of the year, while specialized vessels, insurance premiums and Russian transit fees can erode savings from shorter voyages.
Matthew Wright, an analyst at Kpler, said the route remains poorly suited to replacing established shipping corridors because operators need reliable, year-round services.
Lee similarly expects the Arctic to develop primarily as a seasonal express route for selected high-value cargo rather than a replacement for Suez.
However, climate change could shift the balance in the long-term.
A study published in the WMU Journal of Maritime Affairs projected that melting Polar ice could increase the Northern Sea Route's annual transit capacity to between 127 million and 463 million tonnes by 2050.

articles.title_orig: Netanyahu's political survival on the line as Israel votes
articles.title_zh: Netanyahu's political survival on the line as Israel votes
articles.content_orig:
An extremely tight race into Israel's election Tuesday, has some citizens flying back into the country to cast their votes.
Israel doesn't allow votes from abroad, except from those serving in the country's diplomatic missions. As many as 80,000 Israelis living outside the country are expected to come back to vote in Tuesday's election, according to estimates from one group helping to organize citizens living outside the country. Israel has about 7.3 million eligible voters , according to the Washington-based International Foundation for Electoral Systems.
"While not a large block, the 80,000 that may return home to participate could make a big difference in the final count of a very tight election," said Yael Shomer, a professor of political science at Tel Aviv University.
In Israel's first election since 2022, Benjamin Netanyahu of the Likud party, who has served as Prime Minister for 18 years over three separate periods, is facing top challenger Gadi Eisenkot, the former chief of staff of the Israel Defense Forces, who heads the Yashar party. Both would likely need backing from potential coalition partners in order to win.
Polls are extremely tight heading into Tuesday's election. Issues like security, already a major decider for Israelis, have gotten even more contentious with the Iran war in full swing. The exemption of some ultra-Orthodox men from conscription is also causing a great divide in Israeli society, while Prime Minister Netanyahu is still working on a controversial plan that would give the governing coalition more control over the judiciary.
"All elections in Israel are energetic, but because this one will have such a meaningful impact on the future of the country it has been especially hard fought," Shomer said. "This election is really about how we see our future, voter turnout will be very high."
Voter turnout in 2022 was just above 70% according to Israel's Central Elections Committee. Pollsters believe it could reach as high as 87% this time. Among foreign service workers serving in embassies and consulates outside of Israel, voter turnout was 90%. According to The Central Elections Committee, that number is usually closer to 70%.
In order to help those living abroad come back to cast votes, an organization called Fly & Vote was set up by the America-Israel Democracy Coalition , a U.S.-based group which was originally created in 2023 to stop the effort by Likud to reform the judicial system.
While organizations and political parties are prohibited from paying for any kind of transportation for people inside or outside of Israel, Aid Coalition has found other ways to facilitate the voting.
Fly & Vote, which has been funded by private donations, chartered a flight for Israelis living in Portugal and bought blocks of tickets for flights from the New York area. Anyone on the flights had to pay for their own seats.
"Israelis who don't live here still have a stake in what we do, and we want to help them," said Ora Peled-Nakash, the group's co-founder. "We don't take a political position though and we don't tell anyone how to vote, we just help them cast their ballot."
Travelers will also have plenty of commercial options.
For decades El Al was the only Israeli airline to fly routes from the U.S. to Israel. Arkia started offering flights last year and Israir earlier this year. Legacy U.S. carriers United and Delta are also flying to Israel again after suspending flights due to the war with Iran. Germany's Lufthansa flies to Israel from Europe and British Airways is scheduled to re-start flights this week.
What's more, the price is in line with what it would be during normal times, Peled-Nakash said. There were still a few seats left on El Al flights from JFK or Newark airports ranging from $1,300 to $2,500 as of Sunday, according to research from CNBC.
After years of political instability that saw five elections between 2019 and 2022, Tueday's election result could help shape Israel's political, security and economic direction for years to come. But it also shows how politically divided the country has become.

articles.title_orig: Brazil Supreme Court Orders Flávio Bolsonaro to Hand Over Passports in Money Laundering Inquiry
articles.title_zh: Brazil Supreme Court Orders Flávio Bolsonaro to Hand Over Passports in Money Laundering Inquiry
articles.content_orig:
Far-right senator banned from leaving country as supreme court judge’s ruling makes reference to money-laundering case
The far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro was banned from leaving Brazil and ordered to surrender his passports just hours after his dramatic loss in the presidential election to the leftist president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva .
The ruling was issued by supreme court justice Alexandre de Moraes, the same justice who oversaw the trial of the senator’s father, the former president Jair Bolsonaro, for attempting a coup.
Bolsonaro posted a video saying the decision was based on an interview his brother, Eduardo Bolsonaro, gave last Friday urging his brother to leave Brazil if he lost the election.
On Monday night, Bolsonaro’s party issued a statement acknowledging the election result, saying: “We recognise the presidential result proclaimed by the electoral court, but believe that the questions raised need to be properly clarified through a balanced and democratic political debate.”
Bolsonaro, like his father four years ago, has still not conceded defeat to Lula.
The court’s brief ruling regarding his passport only refers to a criminal case in which the federal police are investigating Flávio Bolsonaro over his possible involvement in a money-laundering scheme . The ruling orders him not to have any contact with his friend Willer Tomaz, a lawyer linked to betting companies that police suspect were being used to launder about £680m.
It also cancelled all of Bolsonaro’s passports, including the diplomatic one he holds as a congressman, and ordered him to hand them over within 24 hours.
Bolsonaro was the first to speak publicly about the matter, before Brazilian media were even aware of the judge’s decision.
In a video posted on social media, he said he had just left a visit to his father, who is under house arrest in Brasília, when “Lula’s federal police were at his door and in the middle of the street, and I was served with an order to hand over my passports and I am also prohibited from leaving the country”.
He added that, although his brother – who is in self-imposed exile in the US – told a US podcast on Friday that he favoured the senator leaving Brazil if he lost the election, “I never said that”.
When his Senate term ends early next year, Bolsonaro will be out of public office for the first time in 24 years, and therefore without the special jurisdiction afforded to officeholders.
He is under investigation in another criminal case, too, over what happened to the £20m he was captured on tape asking a disgraced banker accused of corruption to provide for a biopic about his father.
The Folha de S.Paulo newspaper reported that Flávio Bolsonaro had been persuaded to drop his plan to seek to annul the election, which he had announced after the result was declared on Sunday night.
Bolsonaro had claimed that the two-hour extension of voting – intended to allow voters who had been unable to access the mandatory free public transport to cast their ballots – had harmed the election, despite the fact that his own campaign had also argued for an extension.
According to the newspaper, allies and lawyers told him his argument was legally weak.
Bolsonaro had still not publicly reversed his demand for an annulment, and in the same video he said he would file another case to have Lula’s ticket disqualified over alleged abuse of economic power, a similar case to others his legal team brought during the campaign.

articles.title_orig: JetBlue’s Outlook Worsens as Operating Loss Margin Drops
articles.title_zh: JetBlue’s Outlook Worsens as Operating Loss Margin Drops
articles.content_orig:
JetBlue Airways reported a bigger loss in the third quarter compared with last year, but the New York carrier said strong travel demand is helping to offset higher fuel prices as it seeks to calm investors after shares fell to a new low Monday.
JetBlue stock soared roughly 11% in after-hours trading Monday.
JetBlue on Monday posted a net loss of $257 million for the three months ended Sept. 30, compared with a loss of $143 million a year earlier. The carrier's fuel bill rose 61% to $868 million.
"Resilient demand and strong yields drove revenue well ahead of our initial expectations, allowing us to recapture more of the increase in fuel costs than we initially expected," CEO Joanna Geraghty said in an earnings release. "That momentum has carried into the fourth quarter, and Fort Lauderdale continues to deliver exceptional results even as we significantly grow capacity."
JetBlue's average fares rose more than 19% to $245.11 in the third quarter from $205.67 in the year-earlier period.
JetBlue executives are set to hold an earnings call on Tuesday at 10 a.m. ET, where they will face questions from analysts about the company's long-term health amid sustained losses. A group of the airline's senior creditors is reportedly working with restructuring adviser PJT Partners , the Wall Street Journal reported Friday.
The carrier said it ended the quarter with $2.2 billion in liquidity and that its unencumbered asset base is now $7 billion, including $2.8 billion in aircraft and engines.
JetBlue had total debt of $8.4 billion as of Sept. 30, the carrier said in its earnings filing Monday.
"Importantly, we believe we have the liquidity and financing options to create a strong bridge to at least $1 EPS and positive free cash flow in 2028," CFO Ursula Hurley said in a statement. "We remain focused on disciplined cost execution and capital management as we work toward sustained profitability and positive free cash flow."
Here is what JetBlue reported in the third quarter compared with Wall Street estimates compiled by LSEG:
JetBlue last posted an annual profit in 2019. The airline is in the middle of a multiyear turnaround plan that includes cutting cuts and boosting revenue by investing in premium seats, like a new domestic first class section that recently went on sale.
Fuel costs have eaten into airline profits across the board. JetBlue said travel demand has remained strong despite higher fares , which are up more than 20% this year.
JetBlue has struggled not just with higher costs but also with competition from larger rivals.
It sought to acquire now-defunct carrier Spirit Airlines, but that deal was upended by a federal judge who ruled it was anticompetitive. A judge also blocked a regional partnership between JetBlue and American Airlines , which the airlines argued would help them compete better against carriers in the congested Northeast U.S. JetBlue now has a partnership with United Airlines .
